abstract: Foundation models are typically trained in stages: pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL), with changes in both data and learning algorithms. We show that this algorithmic separation is not fundamental. By deriving suitable RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, we place all of these stages under a single likelihood-based training algorithm, unified training. This perspective turns the foundation-model training lifecycle into a problem of choosing which data to train on, in what proportions, and when, with conventional staged training as a special case. We instantiate this framework in a unified training system that mixes static data and RL generations within a single trainer. Across controlled and real-world experiments, unified training improves the accuracy–compute tradeoff and task coverage while preserving broader capabilities, and provides a stronger starting point for continual learning. This work lays the groundwork for a unified science of foundation-model training, connecting mathematical principles, training infrastructure, and the development of model capabilities.

sections.body: The introduction argues that pretraining, midtraining, SFT, and RL are usually treated as separate learning problems. It states that foundation-model training can be viewed as one learning objective driven by an evolving data distribution. Under this view, the design choices are which data to train on, in what proportions, and when, with staged training as one special case. The paper extends Maximum Likelihood Reinforcement Learning (MaxRL) to arbitrary fixed generation policies, so RL targets can be mixed with static data in one loss. The stated contributions are a unified formulation, comparisons of accuracy and coverage against staged training, and analyses of data mixing and compute allocation.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Foundation-model training stages can be unified under one likelihood objective, with data mixture as the main design choice.

sections.body: This section defines the two objectives used throughout. Maximum likelihood estimation minimizes the negative log-likelihood of prompt-completion pairs. Pretraining, midtraining, and SFT use this loss with static data, with empty prompts for the first two. For a fixed data distribution, it differs from the expected forward KL divergence only by a constant, so both have the same gradient. Reinforcement learning instead maximizes expected reward, where the basic setting uses rewards of 0 or 1. REINFORCE estimates this policy gradient from sampled completions. PPO and GRPO add choices for advantage estimation, reward normalization, and constraints on policy updates.
sections.heading: Preliminaries
sections.headline: Maximum-likelihood loss and the expected-reward policy gradient are set out as the two starting objectives.

sections.body: This section writes RL as likelihood fitting. For binary rewards, the MaxRL gradient equals an expectation over success-conditioned completions, so each update fits the current policy's success-conditioned distribution with the target held fixed. Pretraining, midtraining, SFT, and RL are then each specified by a prompt distribution and a target distribution. Unified training fits a mixture of these sources with mixture weights, and staged training places all weight on one source at a time. Completions from a separate fixed policy can also form a target, but the resulting update is generally not the current-policy MaxRL gradient. REINFORCE and the continuous-reward TailRL objective fit analogous targets with different prompt weights.
sections.heading: A Unified Likelihood View of Foundation-Model Training
sections.headline: RL objectives reduce to maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated targets, so static and generated data share one loss.

sections.body: Each training example is a token sequence with per-token loss weights. Pretraining and midtraining use unit weights. SFT uses unit weights on demonstration tokens and zero weights on prompt tokens. RL gives each correct completion a weight equal to one over the sampled pass rate, and incorrect completions get zero. The authors state that this weighting is the finite-sample form of MaxRL. A generator uses a recent copy of the weights to write RL data into a shared buffer that also holds static data. The trainer samples the buffer by target token fraction and publishes its weights every `k` updates, so generation and optimization run asynchronously. Section D.6 reports the resulting policy staleness and training throughput.
sections.heading: Practical Implementation
sections.headline: A shared buffer, one token-weighted loss, and asynchronous generation implement the unified trainer.

sections.body: The experiments cover a controlled reasoning-puzzle setting and a real-world mathematical setting. The controlled model has 124M parameters and trains on a 20B-token pretraining corpus and a 510M-token midtraining corpus, with 6000 RL updates for Base and 12000 for Extended. The best unified configurations outperform staged training on accuracy in both settings and on generalization to larger puzzles. The unified runs keep retention similar to the pretrain-only model, which the best staged configuration does not. In the 0.76B-parameter real-world setting, mixing midtraining data during RL lowers held-out loss and raises SciQ accuracy, while Coding accuracy declines with more midtraining data. The authors describe the experiments as small-scale.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: In controlled reasoning tasks unified training gains accuracy and generalization, while compute-optimality depends on budget and metric.

sections.body: Related work is grouped into four areas. The first covers foundation-model training pipelines, open recipes, scaling studies, and data-mixture optimization. The second covers hybrid offline and online RL, where prior data is combined with online interaction. Methods such as InstructGPT add a pretraining likelihood term to PPO. The third connects RL with supervised learning through expectation-maximization and weighted regression, including self-training methods such as STaR and ReST-EM. The fourth covers asynchronous RL systems that separate generation from training. The authors say their work differs by placing static and generated data under one likelihood objective, rather than adding a separately weighted supervised term to the RL loss.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work spans foundation-model training pipelines, hybrid offline and online RL, and reward-guided self-training.

sections.body: The discussion states several limits. The experiments do not identify a universally preferred mixture or schedule, and the compute study does not establish scaling laws with predictive power. The analyses have not been extended across model sizes and data budgets. The authors also state that optimization under different data schedules and mixtures is not studied in depth. Most runs optimize a single RL task, so joint training across tasks remains open. Downstream adaptation will still require a separate training stage, and the continual-learning evidence covers only short task sequences. The authors frame data allocation across training as a coupled learning problem for future work.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Open questions remain on choosing mixtures and schedules, scaling, optimization, multi-task training, and larger scale.

sections.body: Appendix A gives the data-mixing and compute conventions. For reasoning puzzles, it lists the midtraining token fraction for each number of midtraining sequences per update. It defines the four mixing schedules and the two loss normalizations compared in Section C.9. Midtraining examples added during RL are converted into passes over the corpus. The compute estimate charges 6N per training token and 2N per generated token, with the RL term written as 8N per token. The remaining material derives baseline-invariance and reward-scaling results for policy gradients and the continuous-reward objective, and states that these identities concern expected on-policy gradients.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers data-mixing and compute conventions, loss normalization, derivations for policy-gradient baselines and continuous rewards, and supplementary results.
